extracted.intended_audience: law students, judges, and legal practitioners studying English/common law and legal history
extracted.subtask_description: Expository guidance on what constitutes the laws of England: the distinction between unwritten (common) and written (statute) law, sources and authority for customs and precedents, and the standards by which particular customs and equitable considerations are recognized and applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of equity
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity is 'the correction of that, wherein the law (by reason of its universality) is deficient.' It arises from interpreting laws by their reason to except circumstances the legislator would have excepted had they been foreseen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity depends essentially on the particular circumstances of each case and thus admits no fixed precepts; it corrects universal laws where they are deficient. But equitable discretion must be limited so judges do not become legislators; equity without law leads to confusion. Example: the law favoring those who stay with a ship in a storm does not apply to a sick passenger who could not leave and thus did not exhibit the valor the law intended to encourage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between lex non scripta and lex scripta
rubrics_metrics.description: The municipal law of England divides into the lex non scripta (unwritten or common law) and the lex scripta (written or statute law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lex non scripta includes general customs (common law), particular local customs, and certain laws observed only in particular courts. Lex scripta consists of acts of parliament and other formally written enactments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three kinds of unwritten law
rubrics_metrics.description: The unwritten/common law properly divides into: (1) general customs (the common law proper), (2) particular customs (local to districts), and (3) particular laws adopted by custom in certain courts/jurisdictions (e.g., civil and canon law usage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each kind has different reach: general customs govern the whole realm (inheritance, property transfer forms, remedies, offenses); particular customs affect only inhabitants of particular districts (gavelkind, borough-english); particular court customs apply within specified jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources and evidence of common law
rubrics_metrics.description: Unwritten law is evidenced by records of courts, books of reports and judicial decisions, and authoritative treatises of learned authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial decisions (records and reports) are the principal evidence of customs and rules of the common law. Reports (year books, later reporters) serve as indexes and explanations of records; venerable treatises (e.g., Littleton, Coke) are also cited as authority. Caution: private reports may contain inaccuracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of precedent (stare decisis) and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions of courts are to be followed as evidence of common law; judges are generally bound to abide by former precedents to maintain legal stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedent should be followed unless it is 'flatly absurd or unjust' or contrary to divine law. If a prior determination is manifestly unreasonable, later judges may declare that the former decision was not law (i.e., was mistaken). Judges are to expound and maintain law, not to make new law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges as depositaries and qualifications for judging law
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges are the depositaries of the law, deriving knowledge from study, long experience, and familiarity with prior judicial decisions ('viginti annorum lucubrationes').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges are sworn to decide according to the law of the land, relying on records, reports, and learned writings. Their role is to determine and apply established customs and precedents rather than impose personal views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisites for validity of a particular custom
rubrics_metrics.description: To be a good (binding) private custom it must meet several requisites enumerated by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The requisites listed are: (1) Antiquity - used so long that 'the memory of man runneth not to the contrary' (time immemorial); (2) Continuity - continually used (interruption of the right destroys custom; interruption of mere possession may not); (3) Peaceable acquiescence - not subject to contention; (4) Reasonableness - must not be legally unreasonable (legal/artificial reason suffices even if common-sense reason is obscure); (5) Certainty - sufficiently certain or capable of being made certain ('id certum est, quod certum reddi potest'); (6) Compulsory nature - not left to individual option (must bind inhabitants); (7) Consistency - must not contradict other established customs. Examples and anti-patterns: a custom permitting cattle in the commons only on a particular day may be valid even if reason is obscure; a custom requiring tenants to act only at the lord's pleasure is unreasonable and void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof and pleading rules for customs
rubrics_metrics.description: Different customs have different rules for proof and pleading in court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some customs (gavelkind, borough-english) are notice-taken by law and need not be proved as to existence, only that the land is subject to them. Other private customs must be specially pleaded and then proved both as to existence and as to the land or matter being within the custom. Trial is generally by a jury of twelve (unless the custom has been previously tried and recorded). London customs are an exception: their existence is proved by certificate from the lord mayor and aldermen via the recorder (except where the corporation has a direct interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and limits of customs derogatory to the common law
rubrics_metrics.description: Customs that derogate from the common law are construed strictly and are narrowly applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customary privileges (e.g., gavelkind enabling certain conveyances) are limited to the exact form authorized by custom; no broader rights are implied. Special customs must also yield to the king's prerogative (e.g., royal succession overrules gavelkind on lands held by the crown).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of statutes on customs
rubrics_metrics.description: An express act of parliament disproves a custom that could not have existed at the statute's date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A statute is proof of a time when a particular custom did not exist; therefore a custom cannot prevail against an express parliamentary enactment. Statutes are part of lex scripta and have primacy over conflicting customs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of mercantile/custom of merchants (lex mercatoria)
rubrics_metrics.description: The custom of merchants (lex mercatoria) is recognized as a system of particular customs used among merchants and is valid for the benefit of trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial usage enjoys high validity in commercial transactions; courts will give effect to mercantile custom on the principle that each trade is to be trusted in its own art ('cuilibet in sua arte credendum est').

rubrics_metrics.name: Status of civil and canon law within England
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil and canon law have effect in England only insofar as they have been received by immemorial usage in particular courts or have been introduced by parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These foreign writings are not authoritative merely because they were codified elsewhere; their force in England depends on local reception or parliamentary adoption. The statute 25 Hen. VIII. c. 21 is cited to emphasize that England recognizes no foreign legislative superiority except by sufferance and long use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and limitations of reports and learned treatises
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports and treatises (year books, Coke's reports, Glanvill, Bracton, Littleton, etc.) are highly respected evidence of the common law, but their reliability varies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancient and authoritative reports and treatises are cited as evidence of settled principles; some reporters (e.g., Coke) are so authoritative that their works are cited by title alone. However, private contemporary reporters sometimes published crude or contradictory accounts; thus care is required when relying on reports and later compilations.
